e.t: This Hebrew word refers either to a diadem, a royal crown-like ornament, or to morning, the beginning of the day. Its precise sense depends on the sentence in which it appears. It occurs three times in the Old Testament: once in Isaiah and twice in Ezekiel. In Isaiah 28:5 it is represented by “diadem,” while in Ezekiel 7:7 and 7:10 it is represented by “morning.” Thus, the word’s normal meaning is recognized through its immediate context rather than through one single English equivalent.

The Hebrew word means “locks,” referring to locks associated with the head. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Song of Solomon: Song 5:2 and 5:11. In these uses, the word identifies a visible feature rather than an action or quality. Its normal sense is therefore a noun naming locks; the surrounding verse determines the precise picture intended in each passage.

This Hebrew word refers to smoke or vapor rising into the air. It is a noun describing a visible, drifting cloud produced by burning or released into the atmosphere. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times across three verses, including passages in Genesis and the Psalms. Its use can describe something seen rising and can also be associated with vaporous clouds. The precise force in any verse comes from the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “ruler,” a person who exercises authority over others. It is used for people in positions of leadership, including those addressed or recognized as “rulers.” In the Old Testament, the word appears 12 times across 12 verses, showing a recurring term for governing persons rather than a title limited to one setting. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or group being described.

d: Karkor , a place East of the Jordan

e.t: Karkor is the name of a place. It is a Hebrew proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Judges 8:10, and the English translations represented here preserve it as “Karkor.” Without the surrounding verse text, its specific setting and significance cannot be explained further; the lexical evidence identifies it as a place name only.

e.t: The Hebrew word means “gall.” It functions as a noun naming a substance. In the Old Testament, it occurs 12 times, all within the Hebrew corpus, and is rendered with this meaning in its dominant usage. Its occurrences include passages involving speech and the giving of something, showing that the word can describe gall as an object or substance within a sentence. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of being “quiet.” It describes a condition marked by quietness rather than speech or disturbance. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 35:20. Its single occurrence makes it a narrowly attested word, but its ordinary sense is clear: it identifies something as quiet. The precise force in Psalm 35:20 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

gl: exalt, get (oneself) up, lift up (self), mount up.

e.t: This Hebrew word describes being raised up, lifted, or placed in an exalted position. Its approved meaning clues are “exalted” and “mounted,” showing that it can express elevation rather than merely movement from one place to another. It occurs six times in the Old Testament, including passages where the wording is rendered “exalted” and others where it is rendered “mounted.” The surrounding verse determines the precise sense in each occurrence.

gl: to undulate (as the earth, the sky, etc.; also a field of grain), particularly through fear; specifically, to spring (as a locust)
make afraid, (re-) move, quake, (make to) shake, (make to) tremble.
d: to undulate (as the earth, the sky, etc.; also a field of grain), particularly through fear; specifically, to spring (as a locust)

e.t: “Shake” is a Hebrew verb expressing the action of shaking. It can describe movement affecting the earth, people, cities, or other created things, especially in poetic and prophetic passages. The word appears 30 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring picture of powerful motion or disturbance rather than a fixed object or person. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being shaken and the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “praised” and functions as an action word describing the honoring of someone or something. In its five occurrences in the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears in Daniel, including statements directed toward God and references to people praising gods or objects. Its role is therefore verbal: it expresses the act of giving praise rather than naming the person or thing receiving it. The surrounding verse determines who is praised and why.

gl: seven (as the sacred full one); also (adverbially) seven times ; by implication, a week ; by extension, an indefinite number
d: seven (as the sacred full one); also (adverbially) seven times ; by implication, a week ; by extension, an indefinite number

e.t: This Hebrew word means “seven,” the number that follows six. It is used throughout the Old Testament for counting people, objects, periods, and repeated measures. The word occurs 394 times in the Hebrew Bible, so its ordinary sense is straightforward and broad: it identifies the quantity seven. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on what is being counted or measured there.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. Its precise English meaning cannot be stated confidently from the available lexical information alone. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 92:11, but the reference by itself does not explain the word’s role or force in that verse. The surrounding verse text would be needed to clarify what it describes or expresses there. For now, the safest conclusion is that this is a rare Hebrew word whose meaning must be determined from its immediate scriptural setting.

This Hebrew word refers to “lime,” a material mentioned in the Old Testament. It occurs four times in the Hebrew corpus, appearing twice in Deuteronomy and once each in Isaiah and Amos. The word identifies the material itself rather than an action or quality. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary meaning is the substance called lime.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a large amount or a group of people, expressed by the approved meanings “abundance” and “company.” It can describe plentifulness generally, or a gathered multitude when the emphasis is on people. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in passages from 2 Kings, Job, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its exact sense in any verse depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes quantity or a gathered group.

e.t: This Hebrew verb means “hired,” describing the act or condition of bringing someone into service for a purpose. It occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both in Hosea 8:9–10. Its repeated rendering points to a consistent idea of hiring rather than a broad range of unrelated meanings. The precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the word itself centers on someone being engaged for service.

d: a Buzite or descendant of Buz

e.t: “Buzite” is a noun used as a personal designation. It identifies an individual referred to by this name or title in the Hebrew text. This word occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in Job, at Job 32:2 and Job 32:6. Its use is connected with the person Elihu and with the speech section in which he is introduced and begins speaking. The word itself supplies identification rather than describing an action, quality, or command.
